claims.assertion: The only off-route segment ran 09:07–09:14 and added 4.67 km (5.77 km driven vs 1.10 km optimal), so the trip's 4.8 km excess under RD-1 is attributable to that single segment.

The driver sent the reroute proposal in-app at 09:03, before/at the start of the 09:07 segment, naming Marina Boulevard ('mind if I go round via Marina Boulevard?'), which satisfies the notice requirement of RD-5.

MARINA BOULEVARD and MARINA LINK are among the roads driven on the segment, so if the rider's silence is read as acknowledgment, the named road agreed is the road actually driven (RD-5 road-name check).

The replaced part of the recommended route was genuinely congested: New Bridge Road was in speed band 2 (10–19 km/h) from 08:54 to 09:14, active before and during the segment, which is a traffic reason under RD-4. (The review note in this brief weighs whether that alone is enough.)

Because the record does not show a rider refusal before the segment (the fare/chat records show only the driver's question), the segment is at worst a no-objection case; under the RD-2 matrix a no-traffic-reason reroute refunds only the excess distance fare, not the full fare, so any order should not exceed the $6.77 excess-distance figure.

The refundable excess-distance fare on the record is $6.77 (4.80 km × $1.4097/km), and RD-2 refunds distance only — not time, platform fee or the metered base — so the maximum exposure on this ticket is that figure.

There is no surge component (multiplier 1.0×) and no waiting charge, so nothing in the fare is attributable to a surge or waiting dispute; the rider's 'higher than estimate' grievance is purely the deviation.

The driver has a long, clean-standing record (5.2 years, 4.91 rating, 347 trips) and the traffic data show no route incident or adverse weather, so the reroute was a routine congestion avoidance rather than an off-app errand or driver-chosen detour for his own benefit.

Any finding against the driver should at most attract the RD-7 remedy — a reminder and a log entry, with no formal warning for a first notification-related incident — and not RD-6 account flagging, as the 90-day record shows no prior notification failure on this trip's facts.

weaknesses: The rider's own complaint (the only rider statement of record) says he 'did not reply' to the driver's question, and the chat record ends at F7 with no rider reply — so the driver's written assertion of 'no objection' (F9) is a statement contradicted by the silence in the chat record, and RD-5 requires that the rider 'acknowledged'.
The driver's statement F9 claims agreement while F7 is the sole chat message and F8 confirms the record is complete and timestamped — there is no rider acknowledgment anywhere in the exchange.

On the merits the deviation is large: F1 shows +4.8 km (+58%) and F3 shows a 4.67 km segment that diverges up to 2,563 m from the optimal route, which the reviewer will see as the classic uninformed-reroute fact pattern in DISP-001 and PREC-1 (DISP-2026-0089, $3.20; DISP-2026-0142, $3.20).

The claim that the reroute was chosen for traffic (F10: New Bridge Road band 2, 08:54–09:14) is contestable: F13 records no traffic incidents near the route, the chosen route's own corridor facts F11 (Sentosa Gateway band 4) and F12 (Kampong Bahru Road band 5) show fast-moving roads, and RD-4 requires the traffic to be on the replaced part of the recommended route — the reviewer may find the driver simply preferred the Marina corridor.
The rider's profile (F15) shows an 830-day account, 4.8 rating and zero upheld disputes, so there is no credibility discount available against the rider.

The driver's own profile (F16) shows two prior upheld route deviations, which, if this segment is upheld, makes RD-6 account flagging live once the current deviation is upheld — so the reference to RD-7 in D9 may not hold if the reviewer counts the earlier upheld deviations as 'repeated' breaches.

The driver's statement that 'no objection, so I took it' is a claim, not consent: RD-5 requires in-app chat or a call recording showing rider acknowledgment, and a rider's silence is not acknowledgment.

Even on the driver's own traffic reason — congestion on New Bridge Road at band 2 (10–19 km/h) from 08:54–09:14, confirmed by the traffic data — there was no rider agreement, so the segment is not exempt and the excess distance fare must be refunded.

There is no surge component (multiplier 1.0×) and no waiting charge, so nothing in the fare is attributable to a surge or waiting dispute; the rider's 'higher than estimate' grievance is purely the deviation.

Any finding against the driver should at most attract the RD-7 remedy — a reminder and a log entry, with no formal warning for a first notification-related incident — and not RD-6 account flagging, as the 90-day record shows no prior notification failure on this trip's facts.

notices.text:

On the part where the driver went a different way, the driver asked in the app but you never replied, and a silent chat isn't an agreement, so that extra distance shouldn't have been charged.

You'll get $6.77 back for the extra distance. It goes to the same payment method you used, and no action is needed from you. Base fare, time fare, platform fee and tolls stay as billed.

Nothing changes on your account — your history is clean, so this is just a fare correction.

We reviewed the route on this trip. It ran about 13.1 km against a best route of about 8.3 km, and the extra distance fell in one stretch where you asked the rider about going via Marina Boulevard. The rider never replied, and no reply isn't agreement — a note after the trip can't stand in for that.

So $6.77 of the distance fare is being refunded to the rider, and a route violation is recorded on your account. Both count against the repeat-deviation threshold, so your account is flagged and you'll get a reminder about the duty to inform riders before you change route.

More than one upheld deviation in a short window puts your account under review.
